opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The bitter lesson, as Rich Sutton put it, is that general methods that scale with compute end up beating approaches where we hand-encode human knowledge into the system. And I think prompting is going through its own version of that right now.

If you look at how people prompt today, there's a lot of hand-crafting. People write these long, elaborate prompts full of little tricks: "think step by step," "you are an expert in X," specific phrasings that happened to work on one model version. It's essentially feature engineering again, just in natural language. And just like feature engineering, it's brittle. You change the model, and half of those tricks stop working or even hurt you.

So the bitter-lesson view says: stop investing so much human effort in the exact wording, and instead build systems where the prompt itself is something you can optimize. You declare what you want, meaning the inputs, the outputs, and what success looks like through some metric or a set of examples, and then you let an optimizer, which is often an LLM itself, search over instructions and few-shot demonstrations. That approach scales with compute and with better models, while hand-written prompts don't.

The other side of it is that models keep getting better at following intent. A lot of what we used to coax out with clever prompting gets absorbed into the model through training: reasoning, tool use, formatting. So the stuff that's worth specifying is less about how to say it and more about what you actually want: your task definition, your constraints, your data, your evaluation. That's the durable part. The clever phrasing is the part the bitter lesson will eventually wash away.

So my practical advice is to treat prompts less like artisanal artifacts and more like parameters in a program. Keep your specification clean and high-level, invest in good evals, and let the optimization and the models do the heavy lifting. That's the bet that has tended to win historically, and I don't see why prompting would be the exception.

r001.rationale: It contrasts step-prescribing prompt tricks such as “think step by step” with the bitter lesson’s preference for scalable methods over hand-encoded human knowledge.

r002.rationale: It says hand-crafted prompting is brittle: changing the model can make tricks stop working or even hurt.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so the bitter lesson, the way Rich Sutton framed it, is basically that every time we try to bake in our own human intuitions about how a problem should be solved, we eventually get beaten by approaches that just scale compute and learn from data. And I think prompting is going through exactly that cycle right now.

If you look at the early days of prompt engineering, people were writing these very elaborate, hand-tuned prompts. "You are a world-class expert," add this phrase, add that phrase, think step by step, put the instructions in this exact order. And a lot of that worked, but it was fragile. You'd change the model version and the prompt would break. You'd move to a different model and all your tricks would stop working. That's the human-knowledge-encoded-into-the-system pattern that Sutton warned about.

What we've seen is that as models get more capable, a lot of that scaffolding becomes unnecessary or even counterproductive. A stronger model doesn't need you to tell it to reason step by step; it already does that. So the lesson I take from it is that the prompt should carry the information the model genuinely can't know, your intent, your constraints, your data, your definition of success, and not your theory of how the model should think. The "how" is exactly the part that gets washed out by scale.

The other piece is that prompting itself is becoming a learned thing. Rather than a human iterating on a prompt by hand, you have an optimizer, often another model, searching over prompts against an eval set. That's the bitter lesson applied one level up. Humans are good at specifying what good looks like; we're not great at guessing which wording of a system prompt will produce it. So you let the system search.

Where I'd push back a little is that the bitter lesson doesn't say humans contribute nothing. It says the durable contribution is in the objective and the data, not in the hand-crafted heuristics. So I tell people, invest your effort in evals and in clearly articulating the task. Treat the prompt as a disposable artifact that you expect to regenerate every time the model changes. That's the version of prompt engineering that survives the bitter lesson.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts hand-crafted instructions such as “think step by step” with the bitter lesson’s warning that human-encoded intuitions are eventually surpassed by scaling compute and learning from data.

r002.rationale: It says elaborate hand-tuned prompts were fragile: changing the model version or switching models could make the prompt tricks stop working.

astra-6.text:
I think the bitter lesson suggests that we should be careful about encoding too much of our own approach into a prompt. It’s tempting to tell a model, “First do this, then do that,” because that’s how we think the problem should be solved. And that can help with a particular model today. But it can also constrain a more capable model to a strategy that isn’t actually the best one.

So I’d distinguish between specifying what we want and specifying exactly how to get there. Giving the model a clear objective, relevant context, and a way to check its answer seems more durable than prescribing every reasoning step. As models improve, we should keep revisiting those instructions and asking whether they’re still helping.

That doesn’t mean prompting goes away. It means the emphasis shifts toward communicating the problem well and letting the model discover more of the solution.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts step-by-step prompts based on how humans think a problem should be solved with the risk that those prompts constrain a more capable model.

r002.rationale: It says a prescribed strategy may help a model today but can constrain better models, and that specifying objectives is more durable—communicating that step-prescribing prompts can become brittle as models improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the bitter lesson is a useful lens here. When we prompt a model, we often try to encode our own understanding of how it should solve the problem: follow these steps, consider these cases, reason in this particular way. That can help, but we should be careful about assuming that our process is the best process for the model.

The bitter lesson suggests that methods that can improve with more computation tend to win over methods built around a lot of human knowledge. So, with prompting, I’d distinguish between specifying what we want and prescribing exactly how to get there. Giving the model a clear objective and a way to check its answer may be more powerful than writing an increasingly elaborate set of instructions.

That doesn’t mean prompting goes away. It means the role of prompting may shift toward defining the task, the constraints, and what success looks like, while letting the model learn more of the strategy.

r001.rationale: It contrasts prescribing steps based on human understanding with the bitter lesson’s caution that human-designed methods may not be best for models.

r002.rationale: It says elaborate instructions may be less powerful, but does not claim that step-prescribing prompts make the approach brittle.
